title: Navigating the Amendments: A Deep Dive into the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026
content:
# Navigating the Amendments: A Deep Dive into the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026

Namaste, esteemed colleagues! We're just fresh out of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, and the air is thick with discussions around the recently passed **Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026**. Having been passed by the Lok Sabha on August 6, 2026, and subsequently by Parliament, this Bill is more than just another piece of legislation; it’s a strategic move by the government to align our fiscal and regulatory framework with evolving global dynamics and domestic aspirations. If you're wondering, "Ab kya change ho gaya?" – trust me, you're not alone! Let's unravel the nuances together.

This Bill, introduced by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, aims to amend several critical statutes: primarily the **Income-tax Act, 2025** (which itself replaced the 1961 Act on April 1, 2026), the **Finance Act, 2026**, and the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**. The overarching goals are clear: attract more foreign investment, reduce compliance burdens, promote domestic manufacturing, and provide greater tax certainty across various sectors.

## Why This Amendment, and Why Now?

You might be thinking, "Just after the Finance Act, 2026, and the Income-tax Act, 2025, why another amendment so soon?" Well, the government's stance is that these amendments are necessitated by "evolving geopolitical developments and disruptions in global trade and supply chains". Essentially, in a rapidly changing global economic landscape, our laws need to be agile enough to respond, encourage investment, and boost key sectors. This Bill also notably repeals and replaces the **Income-tax (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026**, which was promulgated on June 5, 2026.

Let's dissect some of the key amendments, shall we?

## Key Amendments: A Sector-Wise Analysis

The Bill introduces significant changes across various areas, particularly focusing on incentivizing electronics manufacturing, simplifying conditions for data centres, and streamlining the framework for investment funds.

### 1. Boost for Electronics Manufacturing: 'Make in India' Gets a Shot in the Arm

This is perhaps one of the most significant changes, clearly signalling India's intent to become a global electronics manufacturing hub. The government is extending and introducing new tax exemptions for foreign companies engaged with Indian contract manufacturers.

| Old Provision (Income-tax Act, 2025/Finance Act, 2026)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | New Provision (Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Exemption for income of foreign companies providing capital goods, equipment, or tooling to Indian contract manufacturers in customs bonded areas was available until **Tax Year 2030-31**.                                                                                                                                                                              | This exemption has been **extended by a further decade, until Tax Year 2040-41**. The core conditions (foreign company retaining ownership, manufacturer control, production of electronic goods for consideration) remain. A statutory definition of **"specified electronic goods"** has been introduced, covering mobile phones, laptops, servers, hearables, wearables, and their sub-assemblies/accessories. |
| No specific exemption for income from storing components for electronic manufacturing in customs-bonded warehouses.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | **New exemption** for income arising from the storage of components of a foreign company in a customs-bonded warehouse, when these components are for an Indian contract manufacturer producing specified electronic goods. This exemption is available for **15 years**, up to the tax year ending March 31, 2041.                                                                                     |

This extension and the new exemption are a fantastic move, providing long-term certainty for foreign OEMs to commit their supply chains to India. Ab foreign companies will have more confidence in our manufacturing ecosystem, won't they?

### 2. Streamlining Data Centre Operations: Powering India's Digital Future

As India rapidly embraces digital transformation, data centres are crucial. The Bill simplifies the tax exemption for foreign companies procuring services from specified data centres in India.

| Old Provision (Income-tax Act, 2025)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | New Provision (Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Exemption for income of specified foreign companies procuring services from specified data centres. Conditions included the foreign company being notified by the central government, and the data centre being set up under an approved scheme and notified. Exemption generally applied if the data centre was *owned* and operated by an Indian company. | The Bill **removes the notification conditions** for both the foreign company and the data centre. Crucially, the exemption is now extended to cover cases where an Indian company **leases and operates** a specified data centre, not just owns it. This will accelerate investments in AI-focused data centres and support large-scale AI data cities. |

This change is a pragmatic step, recognizing the flexible models in the data centre industry. Leasing infrastructure is common, and extending the exemption here will surely boost investments in our digital infrastructure.

### 3. Rationalizing Conditions for Investment Funds and Fund Managers: Making India an Investment Hub

The government is keen on attracting global capital and encouraging fund managers to relocate to India. The Bill makes significant amendments to achieve this.

| Old Provision (Income-tax Act, 2025/Schedule I)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | New Provision (Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The conditions for an eligible investment fund (registered outside India but managed from India) not to be treated as having a business connection in India were quite extensive (e.g., minimum 25 members, maximum 10% participation by a single investor, minimum monthly average corpus of ₹100 crore, etc.).                                                          | The Bill **reduces these conditions significantly**. For instance, it removes the requirements for a minimum number of members, restrictions on a single investor's participation, and the minimum corpus size. The fund still needs to be non-resident in India, resident in a DTAA country/notified jurisdiction, with Indian residents' aggregate investment not exceeding 5% of the corpus, and not directly/indirectly carrying on business in India. |
| Dividend distributed by a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) to a business trust and then passed on to unit holders was exempt only if the SPV opted for the *old* tax regime.                                                                                                                                                                                          | The Bill **removes this restriction**, allowing unit holders to enjoy exemption on dividend income even if the SPV is taxed under the new corporate tax regime. However, the surcharge rate on income tax payable by an SPV of a business trust, opting for concessional rates, has been **raised from 10% to 25%**.                                                                                        |
| Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) and the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) were taxed on interest and capital gains from government securities (e.g., interest at 20%, short-term capital gains at 30%, long-term capital gains at 12.5%). These changes were introduced by the Income-tax (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026.                          | The Bill **exempts FIIs and BIS from paying income tax** on interest earned on investments in government securities and capital gains from the sale, exchange, or transfer of such securities, effective from April 1, 2026.                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

These changes signal a strong push to make India a more attractive destination for global fund management operations and capital, reducing the compliance hassle and offering competitive tax treatment.

### 4. New Exemption for Foreign Rough Diamond Mining Companies: A Gem of an Idea!

In a move to bolster a niche but significant industry, the Bill introduces a new tax exemption for foreign companies involved in the rough diamond trade. A new provision is to be inserted at Serial No. 13F of Schedule IV.

*   **Exemption Scope**: Income from the sale of rough diamonds by qualifying foreign companies.
*   **Duration**: For 15 years, until the tax year ending March 31, 2041.
*   **Eligible Entities**: Foreign diamond mining companies, sightholders, brokers, aggregators, or tender and auction entities.
*   **Condition**: The sale must be carried out in a **Special Notified Zone (SNZ)**, such as those in Mumbai and Surat.

This is a targeted incentive, aiming to formalize and boost India's role in the global diamond trade. Bahut achha initiative hai for this sector!

### 5. Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007: UPI Charges in Future?

This amendment has generated considerable discussion. The Bill makes a critical change to the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**.

| Old Provision (Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007)                                                                                                     | New Provision (Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| UPI and RuPay debit card transactions operated under a zero Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) regime, legally preventing banks/PSPs from charging for transactions. | The Bill **removes the legal restriction** that currently prevents banks and payment service providers from levying charges on transactions made through UPI and RuPay debit cards. Importantly, it **does not immediately introduce charges** but empowers the Central Government to decide, through future notifications, which electronic payment modes will remain free and where charges may be permitted. |

This change potentially paves the way for future charges on UPI/RuPay transactions, depending on government notifications. While it doesn't mean charges are immediate, it certainly gives the government the *power* to introduce them. This is a crucial point for digital payment users and service providers alike.

## Concluding Thoughts

The **Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026**, represents a proactive and strategic legislative effort. By extending tax holidays for electronics manufacturing, simplifying data centre regulations, rationalizing investment fund conditions, and introducing targeted exemptions for the diamond trade, the government is clearly focused on making India a more attractive and competitive destination for global investment and manufacturing.

Of course, the amendment concerning the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**, will be closely watched. While the current zero-MDR regime for UPI has been a game-changer for digital adoption, the flexibility to introduce charges in the future signals a potential shift in policy, aimed at ensuring the long-term viability of payment service providers. This may be a balancing act between user convenience and system sustainability.

As professionals, it's vital for us to grasp these changes to effectively advise our clients and navigate the evolving tax and regulatory landscape. Keep an eye out for the official notifications and rules that will flesh out the finer details of these amendments!
